title: Kamsa sees him everywhere
hook: in Kamsa's prison, a child is moved in secret, and a frightened king can't stop thinking about the next one
carry: smarana: keep the Lord in mind, always
tomorrow: what did the Lord look like the moment he was born?

segments.voice: Yesterday the birth story began: the Earth's plea, Kamsa's sword, and Vasudeva's promise, kept. Your line was avatara: God comes down when dharma falls.

In the prison, Kamsa kills Devaki's children as they are born. The Bhagavata doesn't linger there. When six have died, the text says, a seventh child begins to grow in her. And this time something is done in secret. The Lord, the Bhagavata says, calls on his own power of illusion, Yogamaya, and gives her a task. A child is in danger. Move him.
screen: `A PRISON IN MATHURA.` → `THE SEVENTH CHILD.` → `"MOVE HIM."`

segments.voice: Yogamaya draws the seventh child out of Devaki's womb and places him in the womb of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, living safely in Gokula, a village of cowherds across the river. In the prison, people say Devaki has miscarried. The Bhagavata names the child from that night: Sankarshana, the one who was drawn out. Later he is known as Balarama, Krishna's older brother, and the Lord himself calls him a part of Shesha, the serpent he rests on. Then the Lord enters Vasudeva's mind, and from there passes into Devaki, and she begins to shine. Kamsa sees her glowing and understands: this is the one. But he can't bring himself to kill a pregnant woman, so he waits, and the waiting turns into obsession. Sitting, lying down, eating, walking, the text says, Kamsa saw that child everywhere. Later the Bhagavata draws a startling lesson from this. Kamsa reached the Lord through fear, it says, others through hatred, the cowherd women through love. What counts is a mind fixed on him. Hindus call it smarana, remembering, and it's why a grandmother murmurs a name of God over the stove, in the car and in the checkout line: Kamsa's constant thought, chosen with love instead of fear. Meanwhile the gods come to the cell to sing to the child inside Devaki. Do not be afraid, mother, they tell her. The one you carry has come to protect the world.
screen: `THE SEVENTH CHILD IS MOVED` · `SANKARSHANA: DRAWN OUT` · `KAMSA SEES HIM EVERYWHERE` · `SMARANA: A MIND FIXED ON HIM` · then, large: `THE GODS SING TO THE UNBORN CHILD`

segments.voice: Pick one name of God you love, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, or simply Om, and say it softly under your breath while you do one ordinary task: rinsing a cup, walking to the door, waiting for a page to load. Many Hindus do this all through the day. If you don't pray, choose one word that steadies you. Kamsa couldn't stop thinking of him out of fear; try a minute of it out of love.
The birth. Before it happens, a brother is moved to safety, a jailer can't stop thinking of the child, and the gods come to sing.
Smarana: keep the Lord in mind, always. That's your line. Tomorrow, midnight in the prison. See you then.

screen: `DAY 880 COUNTS.` → `THE BHAGAVATA · 2 OF 28.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THE LORD LOOK LIKE THE MOMENT HE WAS BORN?`

howItsDone: The gods' prayer to the child in Devaki's womb is heard when the Bhagavata is recited, and Balarama is honored alongside Krishna in temples and festivals. Smarana, remembering God through the day, is lived in quiet repetition of a divine name, often on a mala of beads, and in greetings like 'Jai Shri Krishna'.

chat.meaning: Kamsa, afraid of Devaki's child, saw him everywhere: sitting, eating, walking. The Bhagavata says even that fixed mind reached the Lord. Hindus practice smarana, remembering him all day, with love.

notes: All paraphrase. The count 'when six had died' follows Bhagavata 10.2 (hatesu satsu balesu); confirm.
